opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jake. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how people see changes at work, and nothing you tell me will be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. Long as this isn't some tech company thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say who cares. Some guy in a hoodie made a better Google. Cool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. I make my money on the floor. Two weeks on, two weeks off. AI isn't throwing pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Work my hitch, make the truck payments, have fun on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't care, honestly. Feels fine.

S0.say: Who cares. Some guy in a hoodie made a better Google.
S0.think: Nothing changes. AI isn't throwing pipe.
S0.do: Works his hitches, makes his truck payments and enjoys his days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same tech bros overselling stuff again. Ten years? We'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer beginners, whatever. I'm already in. I got my start on the floor because somebody needed a strong back. They still do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing. Work, truck, fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'whatever' about fewer beginners. Don't you worry about guys coming up behind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not my problem. Less competition for hitches, if anything.

S1.say: Same tech bros overselling stuff again. Ten years? We'll see.
S1.think: I'm already in. They still need a strong back on the floor.
S1.do: Carries on as normal: work, truck payments, days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. Let the guys who look down on rig work find out what it's like. And keep the politicians from handing out free money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doesn't touch me. If anything, all those computers need power, which means more drilling. That's good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick up any extra hitches going. Maybe finally pay something off. Probably not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, kind of. Bit of payback.

S2.say: Good. Let the guys who look down on rig work find out what it's like.
S2.think: Doesn't touch me. All those computers need power, which means more drilling.
S2.do: Picks up any extra hitches going and means to pay something off.
S2.feel: Good, kind of. A bit of payback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government better not touch what people earned. If the stock guys got rich, fine, but don't come after my paycheck to pay some laid-off lawyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Drilling's fine in this one. Physical work is untouched. Only thing that bugs me is if they use the crisis to slow down oil. They always find a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every day they'll give me. Ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Ticked off about the politics.

S3.say: Don't come after my paycheck to pay some laid-off lawyer.
S3.think: Drilling's fine. What bugs me is if they use the crisis to slow down oil.
S3.do: Works every day he's offered and rides it out.
S3.feel: Mostly fine, ticked off about the politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no robot can handle a kick on a rig floor. That's when gas comes up the hole fast. And the people building these things don't know what real work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the newer rigs already have machines handling pipe. The iron roughneck, that's a machine that screws the pipe together, and the pipe arm. If those get smarter, they don't need four guys on the floor. They need one guy and a laptop. And I don't have a cushion. I spend what I make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop spending, I guess. Sell the truck if I have to, which would kill me. Try to get on a crew with an older rig where they won't bother with robots for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mad. And scared, if I'm honest, which I wouldn't say to the guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell the guys no robot can do it. But you think they will?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. Saying it out loud keeps the crew from losing it. Doesn't mean I believe it.

S4.say: No robot can handle a kick on a rig floor. The people building them don't know what real work is.
S4.think: Machines already handle pipe on newer rigs. Smarter ones means one guy and a laptop, and I spend everything I make.
S4.do: Stops spending, would sell the truck if he had to, and tries to get on an older rig that won't get robots soon.
